fields.sections.2.exchanges.0.con.words: Bowen grants every proposed mitigation, then argues that temporary ownership of people remains immoral and that invoking divine endorsement merely substitutes faith for moral evidence.
fields.sections.2.exchanges.0.con.critique: Strongest feature: Bowen grants debt servitude, eventual release, runaway refuge, and protection from beating, then isolates temporary ownership as the objection surviving those concessions, directly answering mitigation defenses with unusual charity. Principal limitation: His premise that ownership is immoral rests chiefly on modern condemnation and intuition, without developing the autonomy-based warrant needed to show why even temporary ownership is impermissible independently of prevailing social judgment. Live burden: Bowen must justify that prohibition and explain why divine endorsement cannot supply objective grounding, instead of dismissing appeal to God as faith-based post hoc rationalization because no further evidence appears here. Locked score: The fixed 85 fits a centrally relevant, highly responsive argument whose lucid charitable hypothetical identifies the residual dispute, while evidential warrant remains weaker than coherence, precision, and burden contact.
